title: Policy engine: add Hosted/Dedicated tier mapping to customer config + enforce consistency
author: Jordan Lee
description: Context: as part of the tiered SLO + error budget enforcement rollout, the policy engine and downstream systems need a single, canonical way to classify each tenant/workspace/customer as Hosted vs Dedicated for (a) correct SLI/SLO aggregation, (b) correct alert routing, and (c) safe routing/degradation rules (Dedicated cannot silently “fall back” into multi-tenant Hosted capacity). Today, we infer “dedicated-ness” from a few different config fields (pool bindings, contract flags, and legacy tags), which has already led to mismatches in dashboards and a couple of confusing support escalations. This PR introduces an explicit tier mapping in customer config, defines precedence rules for migration/back-compat, and enforces consistency at policy evaluation time. What’s in this PR: 1) Customer config schema: adds customer.tier = {hosted|dedicated} and (for Dedicated) customer.dedicated_pool_id required; supports an intermediate migration state where tier is unset but can be inferred; 2) Policy engine: TierResolver that computes an effective tier and emits structured audit annotations when inference is used; rejects inconsistent configurations (e.g., tier=dedicated but no pool binding; tier=hosted with dedicated pool binding) with a clear error message and remediation hint; 3) Control plane integration: propagates effective tier into request context (policy eval output) so gateway/routing can tag metrics consistently and enforce tier-specific constraints; 4) Tests: golden tests for config parsing + resolver behavior; policy eval tests covering legacy customers; routing policy tests verifying “no Hosted fallback” for Dedicated; 5) Docs: internal doc update describing how to set tier, migration plan, and how this impacts error budget calculations + alert routing. Migration/compat notes: Existing customers without customer.tier continue to work; we infer tier using (in order) dedicated_pool_id binding, contract_type == dedicated (legacy), then default hosted. When inference is used we log a warning with customer_id and config source so we can track progress. The hard validation only triggers when tier is explicitly set and inconsistent with other fields. Follow-ups: once 100% of Dedicated tenants have tier explicitly set, we can remove the legacy contract_type inference and tighten validation. Related: ENG-2421 (budget computation depends on tier dimension), ENG-2423 (routing degradation rules), PM-611 (tier principles), SUP-3950 (enterprise request for documented behavior).
commits: config: add customer.tier enum + dedicated_pool_id requirement for dedicated
policy: implement TierResolver with inference + validation + audit annotations
control-plane: plumb effective tier into policy evaluation output
routing: enforce dedicated tier constraint to prevent hosted fallback
tests: add resolver unit tests + policy golden tests + routing integration tests
docs: update internal reliability config docs with tier mapping + migration notes
review_conversation: Rafael Mendes: This is the right direction. Can we be explicit about precedence when tier is unset? I want to make sure SLO aggregation doesn’t flip unexpectedly if legacy tags change.

Jordan Lee (author): Added precedence order to TierResolver docs + code comments (pool binding > legacy contract_type > default hosted). Also added a golden test case that asserts effective tier for a legacy Dedicated tenant when tags are removed but pool binding remains.
Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated customers, we should fail fast if tier=dedicated but pool_id is missing. Otherwise Support will see “Dedicated” in UI but the system routes as hosted.

Jordan Lee (author): Agreed. Implemented hard validation: explicit tier=dedicated requires dedicated_pool_id. Included error string with remediation + link to doc. Existing customers with tier unset will continue to infer tier and not fail.
Ethan Park: Concern: will this block config pushes for tenants that have both a dedicated_pool_id and tier=hosted (someone fat-fingered)? That’s good, but make sure it’s not a silent behavior change.

Jordan Lee (author): Yes, it blocks only when tier is explicitly set. For existing tenants with tier unset, we just infer and emit an audit warning. Also added a metric policy.tier_inference_used with tags so we can monitor before tightening.
Amara Diallo: Please confirm this doesn’t change the request context shape in a breaking way for gateway metrics.
Jordan Lee (author): request_context.tier is additive; existing fields unchanged. Added a small compatibility shim so older gateways ignore unknown fields; CI includes gateway integration tests.
Aisha Bello: Can we ensure Dedicated never falls back into Hosted when burn spikes? I know routing will handle some, but tier must be available early.

Jordan Lee (author): Added routing constraint test + explicit check in fallback_policy: if tier=dedicated, only allow fallbacks within compatible models inside the same dedicated_pool_id (or fail closed).
Sahana Iyer: Nit: docs mention “tenant” vs “customer” interchangeably; can we standardize?
Jordan Lee (author): Updated docs to use “customer” consistently; kept “tenant_id” only when referencing fields.
release_notes: Internal: customer config now supports explicit tier (hosted/dedicated). Policy engine enforces consistency and propagates tier to request context for SLO/error budget aggregation and Dedicated routing constraints.
